newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Independent TV network under fire in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Independent TV network under fire in Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnia's internationally-funded independent television network has come under fire from hostile state-run media who have alleged misuse of donors' money.

The Open Broadcast Network (OBN), a $10.2 million project linking five TV stations in Bosnia, went on air shortly before postwar elections in September, aiming to overcome ethnic divisions created by 43 months of fighting.

But OBN's offspring -- the TV stations' joint venture "TVIN" -- stopped broadcasting on January 1 after just under four months due to problems with its satellite uplink, TVIN news director Kosta Jovanovic told Reuters.
A Bosnian state television anchorman questioned on Saturday's evening news how a satellite failure could prevent OBN from broadcasting when it was backed by millions of dollars of foreign donations.

The Sarajevo newspaper Dnevni Avaz on Saturday published a detailed account of equipment obtained to upgrade participating local stations and said it could have been bought for half the $408,000 spent.

State television carried the newspaper report and alleged that local stations that contribute to TVIN's broadcast were cheated on the amount of equipment they were supposed to receive through international funding.
Jovanovic said he had the impression that the accusations were a deliberate campaign to discredit the network before an fund-raising meeting later this month in Brussels.
"This is no coincidence that certain media are reporting about a so-called financial scandal in TVIN," Jovanovic said. "A genuine satellite failure has been used as an excuse for this campaign."
The office of the international peace coordinator in Bosnia, Carl Bildt, has been raising money for the project to bring some press freedom to a landscape dominated by overwhelmingly state-run media.
Bildt spokesman Michael Maclay said about $7 to $8 million was needed to finance OBN's two-year consolidation plan.
"It's quite well known that the Bosnian government has not been enthusiastic about this," he said.
All but one of OBN's participating stations are in Moslem-controlled areas of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
Nationalist Serb and Croat TV stations have refused to join OBN. The exception was the Banja Luka studio in Bosnia's Serb republic which joined only recently.

"It is not a popular project because nationalists can't control it. It's something they can't manipulate," a Western monitor in Bosnia said. "It's got to succeed. It will eventually be the only cross-entity broadcast."
